lesson.title: Cadences
lesson.summary: A cadence is the harmonic goal at the end of a phrase: authentic, half, plagal or deceptive.

section.title: What a cadence is
section.p: A cadence is the point of arrival that ends a musical phrase, like punctuation at the end of a sentence. Some cadences sound final, like a full stop; others sound open, like a comma, and ask for the music to go on.

Cadences are named by their last two chords. The four main types are the authentic, half, plagal and deceptive cadence. The final chord of a cadence usually falls on a stronger beat than the chord before it.

check.prompt: What decides the type of a cadence?
check.option: The first chord of the phrase
check.explanation: Cadences are classified by the chords at the end of the phrase: V to I is authentic, a phrase ending on V is a half cadence, and so on. The first chord and the key signature do not decide the type.

section.title: Authentic cadences
section.p: An authentic cadence moves from the dominant to the tonic: V–I, or V7–I, in major, and V–i in minor. It is the strongest way to end a phrase. Authentic cadences are either perfect or imperfect:

list.li: Perfect authentic cadence (PAC): both chords in root position, and the tonic in the highest voice of the final chord.
Imperfect authentic cadence (IAC): weaker than a perfect one. Most often both chords are in root position but the highest voice ends on degree 3 or 5 instead of the tonic.

figure.caption: In C major: a perfect authentic cadence, with the soprano ending on C, then an imperfect authentic cadence, with the soprano ending on E.

section.p: Textbooks draw the line differently. In the narrower definition, used by Caplin and many other theorists of form, only root-position V and I make an authentic cadence, so an IAC is always root-position V–I with degree 3 or 5 on top. In the broader definition of Kostka and Payne, every authentic cadence that is not perfect is imperfect: besides root-position V–I with degree 3 or 5 in the soprano, also V–I with one chord inverted, and vii°–I in place of V–I.

check.prompt: V–I in root position ends with degree 3 in the soprano. What is the cadence?
check.explanation: A perfect authentic cadence needs the tonic in the soprano of the final chord as well as root-position V and I. With degree 3 on top the cadence is authentic but imperfect. A half cadence ends on V, not on I.

section.title: Half cadences
section.p: A half cadence ends on V, usually in root position. It sounds open, like a question, and asks for another phrase to follow. The chord before V can be almost any chord: I, ii, IV or vi, for example.

figure.caption: A half cadence in C major: the phrase stops on V.

section.p: In minor keys, iv6–V makes a special half cadence, the Phrygian half cadence. The bass falls a half step from degree 6 to degree 5, while the soprano rises a whole step to the octave above the bass. Baroque composers often end a slow movement or a slow introduction with it, so that a fast movement follows.

figure.caption: A Phrygian half cadence in A minor: the bass falls from F to E while the soprano rises from D to E.

section.p: British English uses different names: a perfect cadence is an authentic cadence, and an imperfect cadence is a half cadence. Do not confuse the British imperfect cadence with the imperfect authentic cadence.

check.prompt: On which chord does a half cadence end?
check.explanation: A half cadence ends on the dominant, V, and sounds unfinished. Ending on I would make an authentic or plagal cadence.

section.title: Plagal and deceptive cadences
section.p: A plagal cadence moves from IV to I (iv to i in minor). It is softer than an authentic cadence and often follows one, as a confirmation at the very end of a piece; for this reason many theorists, Caplin among them, hear IV–I after an authentic cadence as an extension of the tonic rather than as a cadence of its own. Because the Amen added at the end of many hymns is traditionally sung to IV–I, it is also called the amen cadence. In major keys the minor iv, borrowed from the parallel minor, can replace IV.

A deceptive cadence moves from V to vi (V to VI in minor): the music leads us to expect the tonic and then avoids it. The leading tone still rises to the tonic, which is now the third of vi, so vi usually has a doubled third. A deceptive cadence cannot end a piece: the music has to go on to a stronger cadence.

figure.caption: In C major: a plagal cadence, IV–I, and a deceptive cadence, V–vi. In vi, C appears twice.

callout.p: Authentic: V–I. Half: ends on V. Plagal: IV–I. Deceptive: V–vi.

check.prompt: Which chords make a deceptive cadence in a major key?
check.explanation: A deceptive cadence replaces the expected I after V with vi. IV–I is plagal, and ii–V ends on V, so it is a half cadence.

section.title: The cadential six-four
section.p: Authentic and half cadences are often decorated with a cadential six-four: a six-four chord with the dominant in the bass, on a strong beat, just before V. Over the dominant bass, the sixth and fourth fall by step to the fifth and third, so the upper voices move from the notes of I to the notes of V.

figure.caption: A perfect authentic cadence with a cadential six-four in C major. Over the bass G, C falls to B and E to D.

section.p: The six-four chord has the notes of I, but it does not act as a tonic: it delays the dominant, and the bass, which is doubled, stays on degree 5. Textbooks label it in different ways: I6/4–V, V6/4–5/3, which shows that the chord belongs to the dominant, or Cad6/4–V, as this course does. All three labels describe the same chords.

check.prompt: Which scale degree is in the bass of a cadential six-four chord?
check.explanation: The cadential six-four has the notes of the tonic triad over the dominant in the bass, degree 5. The bass stays on degree 5 while the upper voices resolve to V.

check.prompt: Which cadence ends this phrase in A minor?

figure.description: A grand staff with three four-part chords. The bass falls from the top line of the bass staff to the middle line, then rises one step.

check.explanation: The chords are i, iv and V: the phrase stops on E–G#–B, the dominant, so it ends with a half cadence. It is not a Phrygian half cadence, because iv is in root position and the bass rises from D to E.
